lesson.title: Accidentals, Half Steps and Whole Steps
lesson.summary: Sharps, flats and naturals raise and lower notes by half steps, the smallest distance on the keyboard.

section.title: Half steps and whole steps
section.p: On the piano keyboard, the white keys carry the seven note names. The black keys sit between them in groups of two and three. C is the white key just to the left of a group of two black keys.
The distance from one key to the very next key, white or black, is a half step, also called a semitone. Two half steps make a whole step, or whole tone.
Most neighbouring white keys have a black key between them, so they are a whole step apart. Two pairs have no black key between them: E and F, and B and C. These are half steps.

figure.caption: From C4 to C5 on the white keys. The highlighted pairs, E4–F4 and B4–C5, are half steps; all other neighbours are whole steps.

check.prompt: Which pair of white keys is a half step apart?
check.explanation: There is no black key between B and C, so they are a half step apart. C–D and F–G have a black key between them and are whole steps.

section.title: Sharps, flats and naturals
section.p: Accidentals change a note by half steps:

list.li: A sharp (♯) raises a note by a half step.
A flat (♭) lowers a note by a half step.
A natural (♮) cancels a sharp or flat and gives back the plain note.

section.p: On the staff the accidental is written before the note, on the same line or space. In words it comes after the letter: F#, Bb.

figure.staff: F4/q F#4/q G4/h | B4/q Bb4/q A4/h | C5/q C#5/q C5/h |.
figure.caption: F raised to F#, B lowered to Bb, and C# cancelled by a natural.

section.p: Every black key has two names: the key between C and D is both C# and Db. White keys can have such names too. Because there is no black key between E and F, E# is the same key as F and Fb the same key as E; likewise B# is C and Cb is B.
Two rarer signs move a note by two half steps. A double sharp (𝄪) raises it by a whole step and a double flat (𝄫) lowers it by a whole step: F## sounds like G, and Bbb like A.

figure.caption: F##4 and G4 sound the same, as do Bbb4 and A4.

check.prompt: Which note sounds the same as F#?
check.explanation: F# is the black key between F and G, which is also Gb. E# is the same key as F, and Fb the same key as E.

section.title: Writing half and whole steps
section.p: A half step can be written in two ways. With two different letters, such as E–F or C#–D, it is a diatonic half step. With the same letter, such as C–C#, it is a chromatic half step.
A whole step is written with two neighbouring letters, adding an accidental where needed: C–D, E–F#, Bb–C.

figure.staff: E4/h F4/h | C5/h C#5/h || E4/h F#4/h | Bb4/h C5/h |.
figure.caption: A diatonic and a chromatic half step, then two whole steps.

worked.title: Find the note a whole step above a given note

step.p: Take E. A whole step uses the next letter, so the note a whole step above it will be some kind of F.
E–F has no black key between the two notes, so it is only a half step. One half step is missing.
Raise F by a half step: the note a whole step above E is F#.

check.prompt: Which note is a whole step below C?
check.explanation: The letter below C is B, but B–C is only a half step, so B must be lowered to Bb. A# sounds the same but skips the letter B, so it is not written as a whole step.

section.title: Enharmonic notes
section.p: Notes that sound the same but are written differently, such as C# and Db, are enharmonic equivalents. Which name is right depends on the context: the key, the scale or the interval being written, as the next lessons show.

figure.staff: C#4/h Db4/h | G#4/h Ab4/h | B#4/h C5/h |.
figure.caption: Three enharmonic pairs: each pair is one key on the piano.

check.prompt: Which note is enharmonic with B#?
check.explanation: B and C are only a half step apart, so raising B by a half step reaches the key of C.

section.title: How long an accidental lasts
section.p: An accidental applies to its note and to every later note on the same line or space until the end of the bar. The bar line cancels it. A tie carries it over the bar line, but only for the tied note.
Strictly, an accidental affects only its own octave: a note an octave higher or lower needs its own sign. Careful editors add a reminder, a courtesy accidental, wherever a reader might be unsure.

figure.staff: F#4/q G4/q F#4/q F4/q | E4/q F4/q G4/h |.
figure.caption: The second F#4 needs no sign, because the sharp still applies; the natural on the fourth beat cancels it. After the bar line, F4 needs no sign.

check.prompt: What is the third note of this bar?

figure.description: One bar of quarter notes: a note with a sharp in the third space, a note on the fourth line, a note in the third space without an accidental, and a note on the middle line.

check.explanation: The sharp before the first note still applies to the third space for the rest of the bar, so the third note is C#5, not C5.
